question: Which statement best describes Function identity?
options: React.memo wraps a component so it skips re-rendering when its props are referentially equal to the previous render, using a shallow one-level comparison. It is the consumer that makes useCallback worthwhile, because a stable function prop only matters if something compares by reference. A single unstable prop, a fresh function, object, or array, defeats memo entirely, so all props must be stable.

Every render of a component recreates the functions defined inside it as brand-new objects, even when the code is byte-for-byte identical. Because two function literals are never equal by reference, a handler passed as a prop looks new to the child on every render. useCallback preserves the same function instance across renders while its dependencies are unchanged, giving it a stable identity.

React compares props and dependencies by reference using Object.is, not by deep value, so a new function, object, or array each render registers as a change. This is the foundation of why memoization can silently break: the comparison sees a different reference and assumes something changed. Understanding reference comparison explains when useCallback helps and when it does nothing.

useCallback's dependency array must list every reactive value the function reads; React compares them with Object.is and returns a new function only when one changes. Missing a dependency captures a stale value from an earlier render, while listing too many recreates the function needlessly and breaks stability. The eslint-plugin-react-hooks exhaustive-deps rule catches most omissions.

question: Which statement best describes Referential equality?
options: useCallback memoizes the function itself, whereas useMemo memoizes the result of calling a function; internally they are nearly identical. useCallback(fn, deps) is exactly equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps), with useCallback acting as ergonomic sugar for the common function case. Use useCallback for a stable callback and useMemo for a stable computed value, object, or array.

Wrapping every function in useCallback adds memory and a per-render comparison while cluttering code with dependency arrays that drift out of sync. For cheap children the memoization costs more than it saves, and suppressed lint warnings hide real bugs. The rule is to memoize deliberately, only where a measured re-render or effect problem exists, and let the React Compiler handle the rest.

The dispatch function from useReducer and setState updaters from useState are guaranteed stable across renders, so they can be passed to memoized children directly without useCallback. When many handlers fan out to many children, centralizing logic in a reducer and passing the stable dispatch is often cleaner than memoizing each handler. This avoids a proliferation of useCallback calls in complex trees.
